intelligence.human_view: The seats built flat. They knew the Real Object Law — every element a real physical object — but they did not know how to make one. Shawn's trick is the how, and it is almost embarrassingly simple: take the whole thing, clone it once, put the clone behind, move it right or left just a tad. The clone becomes the glow, the edge, the underglow; the original stays the solid body in front. The layering is the depth. One clone does it — triples are too much, quadruples way too much — because depth is a whisper, not a shout. The proof is the certificate name: round 3 fixed the typed name and the certified face stayed solid purple paint; round 4, built on the clone trick alone, made the name a trophy in both states — obsidian body, chrome edge, purple underglow behind, never the fill — and Shawn's eye said "way better". The charge now is general: use it often, on inputs and buttons and everything, because he wants depth on everything. His honest note stands with it: we didn't know how to do that. Now we do — and every brief carries it, so no seat builds flat again.
intelligence.simple_view: Imagine you draw a beautiful name — but it looks flat, like paper. Now draw the SAME name again, right behind it, just a tiny bit to the side, in a glowing colour — and WOW! Suddenly your name looks like it's popping right off the page, like a real shiny trophy! Just one copy behind does the magic. Two copies is too much. One is perfect!
intelligence.grandma_view: It's like this, love — if something looks flat, you don't throw it away, you give it a little shadow behind it. Copy it once, tuck the copy just behind, nudge it a smidge to the side — and suddenly it has depth, it stands up off the page like a real object. One copy does it; three is too much fuss. Simple as that, and it works on everything.
intelligence.naya_view: Clone it once, put it behind, nudge it just a tad — and flat becomes layered. One clone does it. Depth on everything, from now on, in every brief.
